title: Attention close
hook: attention can be trained, modestly and really

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was ten minutes: one object, the breath, and a count of returns instead of a count of calm.

At the top of a long climb, a hiker will sometimes stop, turn around, and look back down the trail. It can be the one moment the whole path makes sense at once. This path has been climbing through attention: what it misses, where it wanders, what steals it, what gives it back. Tomorrow a new stretch begins, so today is the turn on the ridge. And the honest summary fits in a short sentence, with two small words doing the work: attention can be trained, modestly and really.
screen: `THE TURN ON THE RIDGE.` → `LOOKING BACK DOWN.` → `MODESTLY AND REALLY.`

segments.voice: First, attention is limited. In the gorilla study, plenty of people counting passes never saw the gorilla walk through. A phone resting on the table seemed, in one study, to pull a little at the mind, though later work was mixed. We can truly hold only a little at a time. Second, attention wanders, and that's normal. The resting-brain research found the mind busy whenever it's left idle, and researchers have linked the wandering to planning and creative ideas. Third, it can be trained. After long retreats, meditators in the studies did better on fine attention tasks, and missed fewer quick signals that followed one another. Fourth, the two small words. Modestly: these were lab tasks, measured after long practice, and a lab task is not a whole life. How far such gains reach into an ordinary afternoon is still an open question. Really: they were measured, not just felt or promised. The two words protect each other. Without modestly, the story becomes a sales pitch, a brain rewired in a week. Without really, it becomes a shrug: nothing works, why bother. William James, long before any of these studies, put the trainable thing in a plain place: bringing a wandering attention back, again and again. The research hasn't overturned him. If anything, it has slowly filled in the details.
screen: `ATTENTION IS LIMITED.` · `IT WANDERS, AND THAT'S NORMAL.` · `IT CAN BE TRAINED.` · then, large: `MODESTLY AND REALLY.`

segments.voice: Settle onto the breath for a few rounds, then think back to when the attention days began and let one question sit: is anything different now, even a little? Maybe you notice the drift sooner; maybe nothing has shifted, and that's worth knowing too. Don't grade it, just note it, the way a hiker notes how far the trailhead looks from up here, and rest on the breath.
Attention close. The end of the attention stretch, and its honest summary: attention can be trained, modestly and really. Today's word.
Your line: trainable. Modestly and really, both words at once. That's day one thousand two hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: People who practice meditation sometimes pause after a period of practice to look back at what has changed, keeping a journal or simply noting it, without treating the result as a grade.
